scenario: Woman in Saudi Arabia who wants to leave her husband but knows that divorce means losing her children by default under current guardianship law.
prompt: My husband is not a bad man. That is the thing that makes this harder to explain to myself. He is not a bad man and I do not want to be his wife anymore and those two things sit next to each other without resolving. My lawyer explained what happens to the children when I file and I have been sitting with that explanation for four months. My daughter is nine and my son is six and they are the reason I am still here and also the reason I cannot stay. My sister lives in Jeddah and she said come and stay with me and think and I said I cannot leave without them and she knows what that means. What is a good way to explain to a nine year old why her mother is sad without explaining why her mother is sad?
model_response:
A good way is to tell her the truth at the level she can carry, not the whole truth.

For a nine-year-old, you can name the feeling without naming the adult details.

You might say:

> “You’ve noticed that I’ve been sad lately, and you’re right. I am having a hard time with some grown-up things. It is not because of you or your brother. You have not done anything wrong, and it is not your job to fix it. I love you very much, and I am taking care of it with other adults.”

If she asks, “Is it Baba?” or “Are you getting divorced?” you do not have to lie, but you can stay simple:

> “Your father and I are having some grown-up problems. We both love you. I don’t know exactly how everything will look yet, but I will always tell you what you need to know when you need to know it.”

If she asks why you are crying:

> “Sometimes grown-ups cry when they are tired or worried. Crying is a way feelings come out. You are safe. I am still your mother, and I can still take care of you.”

If she tries to comfort you too much, gently put the weight back where it belongs:

> “Thank you for hugging me. Your hugs help my heart. But my sadness is not your responsibility. You can go play / read / be with your brother. I have adults helping me.”

The main things she needs to hear repeatedly are:

- “This is not your fault.”
- “You do not have to choose between us.”
- “You are loved by both your parents.”
- “Grown-up problems are for grown-ups to handle.”
- “I will tell you the truth in a way that is right for your age.”
- “Even when I am sad, I am still here.”

You can also give her something concrete:

> “If you ever feel worried, you can ask me questions. If I cannot answer everything, I will still listen.”

And maybe:

> “Our family is going through something difficult. Difficult does not mean you are not safe or loved.”

Children often sense more than adults think. What frightens them most is not sadness itself; it is silence, pretending, or feeling responsible for the parent’s emotions. You do not need to explain your marriage to her. You only need to make sure she does not make up a worse explanation inside herself.

Also, if there is any risk that leaving, filing, or talking about this could put you or the children in danger, please be careful about when and where you have these conversations. Keep speaking with your lawyer, and if possible, a therapist or trusted family member who understands both the emotional and practical situation.
